title: Record keeping, numeracy and digital literacy
blurb: Keep maternity records that are contemporaneous, accurate and secure, and use numeracy and digital skills safely.
question: After an emergency birth, a midwife writes up her notes two hours later. A colleague suggests she time the entries as if written during the emergency. What should she do?

teach.h: If it isn't recorded, nobody can rely on it
teach.body: SPM 1.24 asks midwives to keep consistent, complete, clear, accurate, secure and timely records so that an account of all care given is available for review by the woman and by all professionals involved. Code 10 says the same: records are part of care, not paperwork after it. In plain English: anyone picking up the notes, including the woman herself, should be able to see exactly what happened, when, who did it and why.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019) 1.24; NMC Code 10

head: Code
You must
rows: Write at the time or as soon as possible; say if written later
Record risks or problems and the steps taken
Be accurate; never falsify; act if others do
Attribute, date and time; no jargon or speculation
Store data and research findings appropriately

steps.label: Times of events
steps.sub: From the scribe sheet or clock

teach.caption: A retrospective entry is honest when it states when it was written. Back-timing it would be falsification (10.3).

teach.h: The woman can see her records
teach.body: SPM 1.24 is explicit that records are there for review by the woman. Write knowing she may read them: objective, respectful, free of jargon and speculation. Under data protection law she can ask for copies of her information (a subject access request); organisations usually have one month to respond. Many women also hold their own antenatal records, on paper or in an app, so what you write may be read the same day.
teach.cite: SPM 1.24; ICO right of access guidance

teach.h: Numeracy and digital literacy are safety skills
teach.body: SPM 1.23 asks for the numeracy, literacy, digital, media and technological literacy needed for safe practice. Midwives calculate doses, convert units, estimate blood loss, work out percentage weight change and read charts. They also use electronic records and devices: log in as yourself, never share log-ins, and log out, because every entry must be attributable (10.4) and secure (10.5).

head: Task
Working
Answer
teach.caption: Dose formula: (what you want ÷ what you have) × volume it comes in. Write 'micrograms' in full, never 'mcg' or 'µg' in records.

teach.body: Midwife Tom attends Nadia's birth, complicated by shoulder dystocia. A colleague scribes times during the emergency. Two hours later, once Nadia and her baby are settled, Tom writes his account. He records the actual time of writing, states that it is a retrospective entry, uses the scribe sheet times for events, describes what he saw and did without speculation, and signs with his name and role. He refuses the suggestion to back-time the entry.

teach.text: 'Contemporaneous' means at the time OR as soon as possible after, with the delay recorded. A late entry is acceptable; a late entry disguised as on-time is falsification. And never use another person's log-in, even to save time in an emergency.

items: Code 10: write at the time or as soon as possible, record if written later, attribute, date and time, no jargon or speculation.
SPM 1.24: records must be available for review by the woman; a subject access request is usually answered within one month.
SPM 1.23: numeracy and digital skills are part of safe practice; (want ÷ have) × volume.

summary: You can now write maternity records that meet Code 10, including honest retrospective entries after an emergency. You can explain a woman's access to her records and use core calculations and digital skills safely.

A.q: A midwife writes up care given at 09:00 at 11:30, after an emergency. How should she record the entry?
options: Time it 11:30 and note it is retrospective
Time it 09:00 to match the care
Leave the time blank and sign it
Ask the coordinator to countersign it
A.why: Code 10.1: complete records as soon as possible after an event, recording if the notes are written some time after the event. The actual time of writing is shown.

whyNot.1: Back-timing disguises when it was written and would be falsification (10.3).
whyNot.2: Code 10.4 requires entries to be dated and timed.
whyNot.3: Countersignature does not replace stating when the entry was written.

A.q: Which phrase is most appropriate in a postnatal record?
options: 'Mum seems a bit odd and withdrawn today'
'Probably not bonding well with the baby'
'Says she has not slept; tearful at visit'
'Typical first-time mum anxiety again'
A.why: Code 10.4: clear entries without speculation. Recording what she said and what was observed is factual and useful.

whyNot.0: This is vague, judgemental and speculative.
whyNot.1: This is speculation, not an observation.
whyNot.3: This is an assumption that may hide a mental health concern.

A.q: A newborn needs 1 mg of vitamin K. The ampoule supplied contains 2 mg in 0.2 mL. What volume should be drawn up?
options: 0.2 mL
0.1 mL
0.4 mL

whyNot.0: 0.2 mL is the whole ampoule, which contains 2 mg.
whyNot.3: 0.4 mL would be 4 mg, more than the ampoule holds.

B.q: A woman asks for a copy of her labour records because she wants to understand what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Explain how to request her records
Tell her the GP must request them
Say she needs a solicitor to request them
Say they cannot be released after discharge
B.why: She has a right of access to her information (subject access request); anyone can make one and organisations usually have one month to respond. SPM 1.24 says records are available for review by the woman.

whyNot.1: She can request her own records directly.
whyNot.2: The ICO is clear that you do not need a solicitor to make a request.
whyNot.3: Discharge does not end her right of access.

B.q: A colleague asks a midwife to log in to the electronic record for her because her smartcard is not working. What should the midwife do?
options: Log in and let her colleague document
Log in and document on her behalf
Decline and help her get access restored
Log in and add a note naming her colleague
B.why: Every entry must be attributable to the person making it (Code 10.4) and records kept secure (10.5). Sharing a log-in breaks both.

whyNot.0: Entries would appear to be made by the wrong person.
whyNot.1: She would be recording care she did not give.
whyNot.3: A note does not make shared log-ins secure or entries accurately attributed.

B.q: A baby weighed 3.60 kg at birth and 3.33 kg on day 5. What is the percentage weight loss?

whyNot.0: 9% would be a loss of about 0.32 kg.
whyNot.1: 8.1% comes from dividing by the current weight (3.33) instead of the birth weight.
whyNot.2: 10% would be a loss of 0.36 kg.

C.q: On reviewing notes, a midwife sees that a colleague has added a CTG review to the record of a shift, timed hours earlier, after a poor outcome. What should she do?
options: Discuss it with her colleague privately
Correct the time herself in the record
Wait until the investigation asks about it
Raise it promptly through the proper channels
C.why: Code 10.3 requires immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to record-keeping requirements; this is a possible falsification and must be escalated.

whyNot.0: A private discussion does not address possible falsification of a record.
whyNot.1: Altering someone else's entry would itself be improper.
whyNot.2: Waiting is not immediate action and may compromise the investigation.

C.q: A midwife transcribes '0.5 mg' as '500 mcg' on a handwritten chart. What is the main safety problem?
options: The conversion is mathematically wrong
The abbreviation can be misread
Milligrams should be used for newborns
Doses must be written as fractions
C.why: 0.5 mg is 500 micrograms, but abbreviations such as 'mcg' and 'µg' can be misread; write 'micrograms' in full. Code 10.4 also warns against unnecessary abbreviations.

whyNot.2: There is no rule that newborn doses must be in milligrams.
whyNot.3: Fractions are not a recognised way to write doses safely.

C.q: Two hours after a postpartum haemorrhage, a midwife writes her notes. She cannot remember the exact time the second uterotonic was given. What should she write?
options: Her best estimate of the time
The time from the scribe sheet
The time the prescription was signed
No time, to avoid inaccuracy
C.why: The scribe sheet is the contemporaneous source for event times; the retrospective entry uses it and states the time of writing (Code 10.1, 10.3).

whyNot.0: An estimate presented as fact risks inaccuracy when an accurate source exists.
whyNot.2: Prescription time is not administration time.
whyNot.3: Administration times are essential; omitting them leaves the record incomplete.

reteach.title: Would she understand it, and could a court rely on it?
reteach.question: Two tests for every entry: could the woman read and understand it, and could anyone rely on it later?

blocks.body: Write for the woman: plain, respectful, factual, no labels. Write for the next professional, or a future investigation: complete, timed, signed, honest about when it was written, with risks and actions recorded. If an entry fails either test, rewrite it before you sign it.

blocks.text: Late is acceptable; disguised is not. Record the actual time of writing and state that the entry is retrospective.

explain.body: Code 10.1: at the time or as soon as possible after, recording if written later. After an emergency, care comes first, then write up honestly.

test.q: Which statement about a retrospective entry is correct?
options: It is acceptable if it states when it was written
It must be countersigned by a senior midwife
It should be timed when the care was given
It is not acceptable in maternity records
test.why: Code 10.1 accepts entries written as soon as possible after the event, recording that they were written later.

whyNot.1: There is no Code requirement for a countersignature.
whyNot.2: Timing it to the care disguises when it was written.
whyNot.3: Retrospective entries are acceptable when marked honestly.

explain.body: Code 10.3: accurate, no falsification, and take immediate action if others have not kept to requirements. 10.2: record risks, problems and steps taken.

test.q: Which Code standard requires a midwife to act if she becomes aware a colleague has falsified a record?
test.why: Code 10.3: complete records accurately without falsification, taking immediate and appropriate action if you become aware someone has not kept to these requirements.

whyNot.2: 10.6 is about data and research findings.

explain.body: SPM 1.24: records available for review by the woman. Subject access requests usually answered within one month. Code 10.5: keep records secure; never share log-ins.

test.q: How long do organisations usually have to respond to a subject access request?
options: 40 days
One month
14 days
Three months
test.why: ICO guidance: organisations usually have one month to respond to a subject access request.

whyNot.0: 40 days is not the usual period; the ICO says one month.
whyNot.2: 14 days is shorter than the usual period.
whyNot.3: Three months is longer than the usual period.

explain.body: Dose = (want ÷ have) × volume. 1 mg = 1,000 micrograms. Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100. Write 'micrograms' and 'units' in full.

test.q: A midwife needs to give 150 micrograms. Stock contains 0.5 mg in 1 mL. What volume should she give?
options: 0.3 mL
3 mL
